subtype: Wide eyes in wonder and fear [Expressing]
passage: Park note, Monday. Mehak, nearly two, was sitting in the sandpit when a large brown dog trotted by on a lead. Her eyes went wide and she went still. Then she turned and looked straight at my face. I kept my voice calm, smiled and said, “That's a dog, and his owner is holding him.” Her shoulders dropped, and she pointed. I stayed beside her while she watched him leave. Next time we will watch from further away first and see how she feels. 🙂

qa.q: Where was Mehak when the dog passed?
qa.a: In the sandpit at the park.

qa.q: Why did Mehak look at the narrator's face after seeing the dog?
qa.a: She was probably checking whether the dog was safe, and her wide eyes could show fascination or alarm. Her dropped shoulders after the narrator's calm words suggest she felt reassured.

qa.q: What is the narrator's plan for next time and why is it sensible?
qa.a: They will start further from the dog and see how Mehak reacts. That lets Mehak approach the new sight at her own pace.

qa.q: How might the dog owner's calm hold on the lead matter to Mehak?
qa.a: Seeing the lead may help Mehak feel the dog is under control, and the owner's relaxed manner adds to the narrator's calm message.

grounding: A toddler widens her eyes at something new and checks the caregiver's face to decide between wonder and alarm.

subtype: Wide eyes in wonder and fear [Expressing]
passage: A peacock stepped onto the mud path in front of the house, fanning half its tail. Charu, two, stopped with her eyes stretched wide. She held her breath and looked at the huge bird, then swung round to see her aunt Lavanya's face. Lavanya was smiling at the peacock. “Mor,” she said softly. Charu's shoulders dropped, and she took one careful step towards it, then another, eyes still wide, one hand reaching behind her for the edge of Lavanya's saree.

qa.q: What did Charu see on the mud path?
qa.a: A peacock with its tail half fanned.

qa.q: What might Charu have felt when she looked back at Lavanya, and what could it mean otherwise?
qa.a: She was probably checking whether the peacock was safe. Her wide eyes could mean fascination or a little alarm, and her stepping forward while holding the saree suggests both.

qa.q: What could Lavanya do to help Charu enjoy the moment?
qa.a: She could stay close, keep her calm smile, and let Charu decide how near to go.

qa.q: What might have happened if Lavanya had looked frightened?
qa.a: Charu might have taken it as a sign the bird was dangerous and backed away, so the wonder could have turned into fear.

grounding: A toddler widens her eyes at something new and looks to the caregiver for a reaction to decide between wonder and fear.

subtype: Wide eyes in wonder and fear [Expressing]
passage:
Outside a pet shop on a Berlin street, a green parrot suddenly flapped its wings against the window. Bao's eyes went huge. He stopped walking and gripped Elif's finger. Then he turned his whole head to look up at her face.
Elif smiled and bent down. "A bird! Hello, bird." Bao looked back at the parrot, eyes still wide, and took one small step closer to the glass.

qa.q: What did Bao grip when the parrot flapped?
qa.a: He gripped Elif's finger.

qa.q: Why did Bao look up at Elif's face?
qa.a: He was startled and unsure whether the flapping bird was exciting or scary, so he checked her face; her smile helped him feel curious enough to step closer.

qa.q: What would you advise a carer when a toddler looks up like this?
qa.a: Show a calm, friendly face and name the thing simply, as Elif did, so the child can decide it is safe. 🙂

qa.q: If Elif had looked alarmed, what might Bao have done?
qa.a: He would likely have pulled back or cried, reading her face as a warning.

grounding: A toddler's wide eyes at a new sight and his look to the caregiver's face to decide whether it is safe.

subtype: Wide eyes in wonder and fear [Expressing]
passage: I'm Jaya. I run the tea stall by the bus stop, so I see everything. On Saturday a new shop opened, with a man in a lion costume dancing at the door. A tiny girl, Ira, stopped in front of him. Her eyes went so wide I could see the whites. She didn't move. Then she looked up at her mother. Her mother laughed and roared softly. Ira stared a bit longer, then gave the lion a small wave.

qa.q: What was dancing at the door of the new shop?
qa.a: A man in a lion costume.

qa.q: What might Ira's very wide eyes have meant?
qa.a: They could have meant fascination or alarm; her stillness and look to her mother suggest she was unsure, and her small wave after her mother laughed suggests she felt safe and curious.

qa.q: Which reaction of the mother's worked, and why?
qa.a: Laughing and roaring softly worked, because it showed Ira the lion was play, not danger.

qa.q: How might Ira's mother see the moment?
qa.a: She likely noticed Ira looking up at her and chose to show she was relaxed, perhaps feeling pleased when Ira waved.

grounding: A tea-stall owner sees a toddler widen her eyes at a costume and check her mother's face before deciding it is fun.

subtype: Wide eyes in wonder and fear [Expressing]
passage:
Day one at the beach: Hansa stared at the waves with wide eyes, gripping Madhav's neck. He was tense about the tide and held her tight. She looked at his face and started to cry.
Day two: Madhav sat down calmly on the sand and smiled. Hansa's eyes were still wide, but she looked from the water to his face and stayed quiet.
Day four: she ran toward the foam, laughing, and glanced back at him.

qa.q: What did Hansa do on day four?
qa.a: She ran toward the foam laughing and glanced back at Madhav.

qa.q: Why did Hansa cry on the first day?
qa.a: She was already wide-eyed and unsure about the waves, and when she looked at Madhav's tense face she likely read it as danger and felt afraid.

qa.q: What changed between day one and day two, and why did it help?
qa.a: Madhav sat calmly and smiled, so when Hansa checked his face she got a safe signal and could watch the waves with curiosity instead of fear.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel when Hansa laughs by the foam on day four?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and happy, seeing that his calm helped her enjoy the sea.

grounding: Over several days a toddler's wide eyes at the sea turn from alarm to fascination as she reads her father's face.

subtype: Wide eyes in wonder and fear [Expressing]
passage:
The fountain in the middle of the shopping arcade was quiet. Then, with a hiss, it shot water high into the air.
Irawati went completely still in her pram. Her eyes stretched wide. Was she about to cry?
She twisted round to find her Amma's face.
Kavitha smiled and said, “Water! Whoosh!” and pointed up.
Irawati looked back at the fountain. Her shoulders loosened and she leaned forward, kicking her feet, watching every splash.

qa.q: Where was the fountain?
qa.a: It was in the middle of the shopping arcade.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when her eyes went wide, and how did she decide?
qa.a: She was startled and could have been either fascinated or alarmed; she checked her Amma's face, and the calm smile helped her settle into curiosity.

qa.q: Why was Kavitha's reaction helpful?
qa.a: Her calm smile and simple words showed Irawati the fountain was safe and fun, so the wide-eyed moment turned into wonder.

qa.q: What would change if Kavitha had gasped or looked worried?
qa.a: Irawati might have read the fountain as frightening and cried instead of leaning in to watch.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler widening her eyes at something new and looking to her caregiver to decide whether it is wonder or alarm.
